### 2026-10-11 – I finished following the tutorial, however I wanted to add more to the Starbie. Since I have way more experience coding than with the hardware components, I decided to go for a software change instead

**5h**

I finished following the tutorial, however I wanted to add more to the Starbie. Since I have way more experience coding than with the hardware components, I decided to go for a software change instead of a hardware change. After thinking for some time, I decided to add TinyML gesture recognition. Instead of relying on a simple magnitude threshold for shaking, using this I would be able to capture raw accelerometer data from the MPU6050 and train a lightweight neural network to classify specific physical gestures. I would be able to trigger different actions by drawing a circle in the air or some other motion as a replacement of shaking the Starbie instead. To do this, I would first need to collect the data, train the model, add that new library to the original Starbie code, and finally update the code. I did use AI occasionally when I was stuck, however it was a great learning experience, and I tried to do as much as I could by myself.

To collect the data, I created a temporary data collection sketch in the Arduino IDE. I did this to temporarily replace the Starbie firmware with a minimal Arduino sketch that reads accelerometer and gyroscope data from the MPU object at a  fixed frequency (like 50Hz), and had it print the X, Y, and Z values.

I then made an empty project at studio.edgeimpulse.com and installed the Edge Impulse CLI, so that when I assemble the Starbie I can use it. However, for now, to collect the data, I ended up using my phone since I didn’t have the Starbie yet. I ended up settling on these for the gestures for each of the 4 actions:

NAP - moving the board side to side (like rocking a baby)

PLAY - a wrist flick

FEED - doing a tap on the back of the board

PET - two taps on the front

I got the data by doing the action 3-4 times with my phone:

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 12.09.43 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/3a6448d2e403f665f1dcc4c7149a110df75bf028f80df0f46f25b6033723789e.png)

However, after doing the automatic 80/20 train/test split, it wasn't good:

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 12.12.52 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/580cf828afb3d823163b7d436017b17ae913c3c87ce952ea99695394616a337c.png)

So I had to manually split it myself, and I ended up having one of each action in the test split, and everything else as training. After that, I created an impulse for the ML model to learn from the data. This is what I got after generating the features:

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 12.23.51 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/7348cef9593506cd487dd2f42b52f368f8ee6221d6063868df1dbcf12c153052.png)

Overall, it was somewhat split, with idle being all over the place since that was me doing random actions that weren't the intended gestures (basically everything it should ignore). So, I decided to train it and these were the results:

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 1.00.14 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/21ddb76cf3d816dca8cc01aa4a19aac2da0933f188eebf9933982b1fdfed0667.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 1.00.27 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/9e9f66af107424340471182f2c8c433a6cd470547f148a5488f283bf858829a7.png)

![Screenshot 2026-10-11 at 1.00.52 PM](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/7ME5CuFiz5X4u2KxuO278yO001rQ8Db2/88465320422a4fad505b5f7c662f7c57b93e89582afd57d06bace87fa83e1e3d.png)

Since they were pretty good, I decided to keep it and export it as an Arduino library. I then added the library to Starbie.ino. In the code, I updated MPU_READ_INTERVAL_MS from 30 to 16 since my phone recorded data at 62.5Hz and I also replaced the checkForShake function with a checkForGesture function.

Now, all I need to do is assemble the Starbie and test it out!
